citation: Makransky, G., Bonde, M. T., Wulff, J. S. G., Wandall, J., Hood, M., Creed, P. A., Bache, I., Silahtaroglu, A., & Nørremølle, A. (2016). Simulation based virtual learning environment in medical genetics counseling: An example of bridging the gap between theory and practice in medical education. BMC Medical Education, 16, 98. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0620-6
thesis: A single 2-hour desktop simulation (Labster) combining a virtual genetics laboratory with a virtual-patient counseling scenario produces significant pre-to-post gains in knowledge, intrinsic motivation, and self-efficacy among 300 first-year medical/molecular-biomedicine students, with gain magnitude moderated by students' prior knowledge; the authors argue this supports simulation as a way to bridge theoretical medical-science instruction and clinical practice (FE, p.1-3).

sections.title: Abstract
sections.summary: States background, methods (N=300 pre/post), results (knowledge d=0.73, motivation d=0.24, self-efficacy d=0.46), and conclusion that the simulation increased learning, motivation, self-efficacy, and perceived relevance (p.1).

sections.title: Background
sections.summary: Motivates the study via the gap between theoretical medical-science education and clinical practice, and cost/time/safety barriers restricting hands-on laboratory access; frames simulation as a way to close that gap (p.2).

sections.title: Simulation based learning environments in medical education
sections.summary: Reviews prior digital-simulation literature (mannequins, virtual patients, gamified laboratories) showing benefits to skill acquisition, retention, and motivation, noting simulations are rarely applied to basic medical science rather than clinical procedure (p.2).

sections.title: Simulations to bridge theory and practice: medical genetics as an example
sections.summary: Introduces the Labster-built genetics case (pregnant couple, possible chromosomal abnormality); states four study aims — clinical-translation understanding, knowledge, intrinsic motivation, self-efficacy (pp.2-3).

sections.title: Method — Study sample
sections.summary: Entire class of 300 University of Copenhagen first-year students (84% medicine, 16% molecular biomedicine) completed the simulation as a mandatory course component, fall 2014; 54%/40% complete valid responses on optional self-efficacy/motivation scales; no control group (p.3).

sections.title: Method — Training exposure and main outcome measures
sections.summary: 30-min pre-test / 2-hr simulation / 30-min post-test; knowledge via 18 MCQ items, motivation via Intrinsic Motivation Inventory-adapted items, self-efficacy via MSLQ-adapted items, plus 4 Likert items on perceived clinical transfer (pp.3-4).

sections.title: Results
sections.summary: Knowledge 67%->79% correct (d=0.73), largest gain for low-knowledge students (d=3.35); intrinsic motivation (d=0.24) and self-efficacy (d=0.46) also increased significantly; 78-93% of students reported greater interest, motivation, confidence in counseling, and understanding of clinical translation (pp.4-6).

sections.title: Discussion
sections.summary: Interprets gains as evidence for bridging theory/practice, consistent with Cook et al.'s meta-analytic findings on virtual-patient benefits; notes effect strength varied by prior-knowledge group, with ceiling effects for high-knowledge students on knowledge (p.6).

sections.title: Recommendations for practice
sections.summary: Argues for integrating simulations like this one into medical curricula given documented benefits to knowledge, motivation, self-efficacy, and perceived relevance (pp.6-7).

sections.title: Limitations and future research
sections.summary: Flags absence of a control group, reuse of identical knowledge items pre/post, and low completion rates on optional scales; calls for causal-process research on design features (p.7).

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.summary: Reaffirms that the simulation increased learning, intrinsic motivation, and self-efficacy (moderated by prior knowledge) and increased perceived relevance to future clinical practice (p.7).

constructs.name: learning outcomes: retention & transfer
constructs.note: knowledge MCQ d=0.73 (67%->79%); 4-item transfer/relevance Likert battery, 90% agreement, 78% counseling confidence (FE).

constructs.name: affect: enjoyment & intrinsic motivation
constructs.note: IMI Interest/Enjoyment-derived items, d=0.24 overall; significant for medium/high-knowledge tertiles, not low (FE).

constructs.name: self-efficacy
constructs.note: MSLQ-derived items, d=0.46 overall; largest for low (d=0.61) and high (d=0.52) knowledge tertiles (FE).

constructs.name: situational interest
constructs.note: single appraisal item, 82% found the topic more interesting post-simulation; not a validated scale (FE).

constructs.name: learning outcomes: procedural / skills
constructs.note: operationalized loosely via in-sim lab tasks (amniocentesis, array CGH, karyotyping) and counseling-confidence item (FE).

conditions.name: desktop-3D / non-immersive VR
conditions.note: Labster desktop simulation; virtual genetics laboratory (amniocentesis, karyotyping).

conditions.name: screen-based virtual patient / sim
conditions.note: virtual pregnant-couple counseling scenario embedded in the same session.

conditions.name: conventional instruction (control)
conditions.note: NOT operationalized — no control/comparison arm; single-arm pre/post design, explicitly acknowledged as a limitation.

readings: All three primary outcomes (knowledge, motivation, self-efficacy) increased significantly pre-to-post (FE, p.4-6).

Effect size was strongly moderated by prior knowledge: low-knowledge tertile showed the largest knowledge gain (d=3.35) but non-significant motivation gain; high-knowledge tertile showed the smallest knowledge gain (d=0.36, ceiling effect) but the strongest motivation/self-efficacy gains (FE, p.4-6).

Counseling-confidence finding read as corroborating Cook et al.'s meta-analytic conclusion on virtual-patient benefits; authors argue their design adds value by pairing virtual-patient counseling with virtual-laboratory procedure practice (FE, p.6).
Discussion cites Pekrun's control-value theory to explain why weaker students report boredom/demotivation under high academic demand, framing hands-on simulation as a compensating format (FE, p.6).
Authors acknowledge no control group, repeated pre/post knowledge items, and low completion of optional non-cognitive scales as limitations (FE, p.7).

concepts.note: commercial simulation-authoring platform; co-author M. Bonde is Labster's CEO (competing-interest disclosure, p.8).

tensions.axis: media-comparison designs are informative <-> methods-not-media / value-added is the valid paradigm
tensions.note: This unit sidesteps the comparison-design debate entirely — single-arm pre/post with no control condition, a methodological outlier relative to Strand C's comparison-heavy designs; the authors state the comparison question 'has been investigated previously' elsewhere rather than re-running it (p.7).

tensions.axis: simulation beats no-intervention strongly <-> sim-vs-sim differences negligible
tensions.note: Prior-knowledge moderation (ceiling effect for high-knowledge students; largest gain for low-knowledge students) complicates a flat 'simulation causes learning' claim — the effect is population-dependent, not uniform (p.4-6).
